What is the significance of 144Hz? For the best movie experience, it's better to have 120Hz, right?
the higher the Hz, the better the framerate, the better for the eyes and brain, that has to put it together to a fluent motion.
Can you explain what Hz is to me?

Hz (hertz) is the refresh rate of your monitor. Every time your monitor refreshes itself it grabs a new frame from the video card to display. So a standard monitor has 60hz, refreshes 60 times a second, which means it's capable of showing up to 60FPS.
Hz is hertz is cycles per second. So frames per second is almost an identical meaning.

For movies it doesn't matter unless you have software on your computer that creates motion interpolation. This is the rendering of extra frames that aren't really there in an attempt to create smoother video playback. Otherwise, most films are recorded at 24 FPS, so getting 144HZ monitor would be a waste in that case.

HZ is the refresh rate of the monitor, which means each time it refreshes it grabs a new frame. This means that standard monitors that are 60HZ, can't actually process anything over 60 frames a second in video games, because it only grabs frames (refreshes) 60 times per second. Getting a monitor with a higher refresh rate allows the monitor to display frames up to the refresh rate, so it would be able to display 144 frames if it's a 144HZ monitor.

This results in more fluid and lifelike frames (yes, it's a very big difference).

I understand refresh, that wasn't exactly my question. It doesn't only matter with motion interpolation. Some video plays at 60fps (e.g. some BluRay and console systems), some plays at 30fps (e.g. YouTube), some plays at 24fps (e.g. DVDs), and all of those factor into 120. So if you watch a DVD on a 120Hz TV, the framerate perfectly lines up with the TV's refresh, pushing one frame for every 5 frames of the TV. If you have a 144Hz TV, the 30 and 60fps video formats would have refresh artifacts and seem to stutter because the video framerate would not line up with the TV framerate. This artifacting will not be obvious, but I wouldn't think the difference between 120Hz and 144Hz would be obvious either. (though the 48fps VGHS, for example, would not have this problem with 144Hz, but would with 120Hz)

There's not a huge difference between 120Hz and 144Hz, and with how much I watch movies on my computer, I'd prefer the 120Hz, which would still be a huge improvement for me since I'm used to gaming on 60Hz anyway, on top of being (presumably) less expensive.

I just didn't know if there was a particular reason I didn't know of that 144Hz was better for gaming.

tl;dr: faster refresh isn't always better, I just wondered if 144Hz in particular was an optimal frequency standard for gaming.

It is if you count in the fact that alot of shooting games rely on the most accurate depiction possible, which is possible with an uncapped framerate. (not to talk about POV. apart from games settings, screen size, not just resolution, matters quite a bit)

not to mention scrolling and dragging through pages looks and feels alot smoother, and more relaxing.

Films are usually about 24 fps so an "ideal" playback would be 24hz. But as long as the refresh rate is evenly divisible by the 24 fps film source, you should be ok. 24 goes into 144 6 times evenly so you should be ok.

What you don't want is a situation where the display is 30hz and your source is 24 fps. That means you have to repeat certain frames (or do weird blending). It's not terrible, but once you notice it, it's really annoying.

inaccurate. the way that LCD/LED works is by putting light through a set of different layers:

2 diffuseness filters (spreads out the intense lightning, to smoothen it out a bit)

a liquid crystal filter, with an electrode layer, activating certain parts, to make it shine through the right places

the color filter(the small dot matrix)

and two polarizing filters, one vertical, one horizontal, sandwiching in the liquid crystal filter.

the way a LCD/LED display works (only difference between LCD and LED is what it uses as light source), is that it rejects all light that can't fit through the polarizing filters. which under normal circumstances, would be everything
